The Marquette Building, completed in 1895, is a Chicago Landmark that was designed by architects Holabird & Roche. It was designed by William Holabird and Martin Roche, with Coydon T. Purdy, architects of the firm Holabird & Roche.

The building was one of the early steel frame skyscrapers of its day, and is considered one of the best examples of the Chicago School of architecture. The architects, Holabird & Roche, used trademark long horizontal bay "Chicago windows" on the Marquette Building, which are large panes of glass flanked by narrow sash windows.

The building is also notable for its interior design. The hexagonal railing around the lobby atrium is decorated with a mosaic frieze by the Tiffany studio depicting events in the life of Jacques Marquette, his exploration of Illinois, and Native Americans he met. The mosaics are by Louis Comfort Tiffany and his chief designer and art director, Jacob Adolph Holzer.

## System Overview

The Babylonians used a sexagesimal (base-60) number system inherited from either the Sumerian or the Akkadian civilizations. Only two symbols (𒁹 to count units and 𒌋 to count tens) were used to notate the 59 non-zero digits.

## How It Works

The combination 𒌋𒌋𒁹𒁹𒁹 represented the digit for 23. The rightmost group is units (60⁰), the next left is 60¹, then 60², etc. For example, ▼ ◄▼▼ represents (1 × 60¹) + (10 + 1 + 1 × 60⁰) = 60 + 12 = 72.

## Unicode Support

Since Unicode 5 (2006) cuneiform symbols can be represented on compatible browsers. Cuneiform Numbers and Punctuation are found in Unicode Range 12400-1247F.

## Important Characteristics

A space was left to indicate a place without value, similar to the modern-day zero. Babylonians later devised a sign to represent this empty place. However, they lacked a symbol to serve the function of radix point, so the place of the units had to be inferred from context.

# Decoding Babylonian Cuneiform Numbers

## How the System Works

Babylonian numerals use a base-60 (sexagesimal) system with two primary symbols: vertical bars (|) representing 1 and chevrons (<) representing 10. As the page explains, "numbers are written in a cuneiform style with | (pipe or nail) and < (corner wedge or bracket)."

## Position and Value Calculation

The system employs positional notation where "each position represents a power of 60." Spaces separate position groups, so the rightmost group represents 60⁰, the next left represents 60¹ (60), then 60² (3600), and so on.

Economic Crunch is a vanilla ice cream with chocolate covered almond, pecans and walnuts. The epitaph on its headstone reads: "A delightful mash, This flavor we remember For the stock market crash On the sixth of November."

The physical Flavor Graveyard opened in 1997 and originally contained just 4 flavors, which only existed in the United States: Dastardly Mash, Economic Crunch, Ethan Almond, and Tuskegee Chunk.

The day after the stock market crash of November 6, 1987, Ben & Jerry's sent a truck to Wall Street and began handing out free scoops of Economic Crunch ice cream to brokers and investment bankers. ## Alfonso Visconti: Bishop of Cervia

Alfonso Visconti (1552–1608) was an Italian Catholic cardinal and diplomat. Pope Gregory XIV made him Bishop of Cervia on 8 February 1591 with the idea of sending him as Nuncio in Spain.

## His Role in the Catholic Hierarchy

He was consecrated Bishop in Salzburg on 14 July 1591 by Wolf Dietrich von Raitenau. Alfonso Visconti (1591–1601) had been nuncio to the emperor (1589–1591) and to Transylvania (1595–1596).

After his time as Bishop of Cervia, Pope Clement VIII elevated him to the dignity of cardinal in the consistory of 3 March 1599. From 10 September 1601 until his death, Alfonso Visconti served as Bishop of Spoleto.

## His Diplomatic Career

In 1595, Pope Clement VIII appointed Alfonso Visconti, then Bishop of Cervia, as apostolic nuncio to Transylvania to bolster Catholic influence in the region amid the ongoing Fifteen Years' War (1593–1606) against the Ottoman Empire. The mission's core objectives included mediating internal conflicts within the Catholic Báthory dynasty.

# National Geographic's First Hosted Digital Video Series

**Series Title:** "Ingredients, The Stuff Inside Your Stuff"

**Launch Date:** September 15, 2016

**Host:** George Zaidan, an MIT-trained chemist and science educator

**Platform:** YouTube and NationalGeographic.com

## What It's About

The show explores everyday household products by attempting to recreate them using only natural ingredients and no recipe. In each episode, Zaidan decodes chemical ingredient lists, identifies what they do, finds natural substitutes, and constructs DIY versions in his chemistry lab/kitchen.

As described in the announcement: "George will decode long lists of intimidating chemical names, figure out what they all do, try and find natural substitutes and cook up the do-it-yourself versions."

## Episode Topics

The initial season covers 11 products including toothpaste, lipstick, shaving cream, nail polish, gum, air freshener, peanut butter, conditioner, hand sanitizer, dry-erase markers, and gum sweetener. The series aims to reveal the science behind ordinary products viewers typically take for granted.

## Buck Ellison's "Rain in Rifle Season" Photograph

The photograph by Buck Ellison takes as its subject the real-life figure Erik Prince, reimagined as he might have been around the start of the war in Afghanistan. The project focuses on Erik Prince at exactly the artist's age, thirty-four years old, on his ranch near Cody, Wyoming, and is set in 2003.

## Clausewitz's "On War" in the Photograph

One of the most notable details in this artwork is the reference to Clausewitz. He has one finger in a book – Carl von Clausewitz's On War (1832). He casually dips his finger into Von Clausewitz's On War, a double citation of both the Armada Portrait of Queen Elizabeth (in which her casually placed finger denotes dominion over the American colonies) as well as Prince's own claim to have modeled his Afghanistan strategy on the approach of the 19th century British.

## Erik Prince Context

Erik Prince co-founded the security and mercenary firm Blackwater. The company received widespread notoriety in 2007 when a group of its employees killed seventeen Iraqi civilians in the Nisour square in Baghdad.

The photograph was featured in the Whitney Biennial 2022: Quiet as It's Kept (Whitney Museum of American Art, New York, April 6- September 5, 2022).

# Doctoral Thesis Summary

**Title:** "The logic of the liver": a deontic view of the intentionality of desire

**Author:** Federico Lauria

**Defense Date:** February 14, 2014

**Institution:** University of Geneva

## Overview

This doctoral thesis proposes a deontic conception of desire, arguing that "desiring an state of affairs is representing that state as what must or should be." The work critiques two traditional theories—the evaluative view (desire as positive evaluation) and the motivational view (desire as action motivation)—before advancing three supporting arguments for the deontic approach.

## Key Arguments

The thesis develops its position through:
1. The direction of fit principle in desire
2. The death of desire principle
3. Desire's explanatory profile

The research then explores applications regarding desire's normative character and desire typologies while addressing major objections to the deontic framework.

## Affiliations

The work was conducted within the Centre for Affective Sciences and the Department of Philosophy, with supervision by Julien Deonna and Gianfranco Soldati.

The thesis is openly accessible with 48,000+ views and nearly 10,000 downloads on the University of Geneva's open archive.

# "Chapter X, A Living Man Declared Dead and Other Chapters I-XVIII"

**What it is:** A photographic series consisting of archival inkjet prints in six components, created in 2011.

**Creator:** Taryn Simon

**Source:** The work documents the descendants of Cabrera Antero, an Igorot community member from the Philippines. Antero was displayed at "the Louisiana Purchase Exposition, a World's Fair held in St. Louis in 1904." He met his wife during their voyage to America and they eventually had eleven children.

**Title reference:** The title alludes to the concept of being publicly declared dead while living—metaphorically capturing how Antero and his community were treated as spectacles at the fair, yet their lives continued with profound personal significance. The twenty-chapter structure explores how historical moments reshape individual destinies across generations, examining what Simon called "the intersection of personal and social history."

The work tracks Antero's bloodline across decades, photographing his descendants alongside biographical information and historical documentation of the exposition.

# Artwork Analysis: "Heading – Chapter XIII 'Sutter's Gold'"

**The Artwork:**
This is a small-scale woodcut print measuring 2 1⁄8 x 3 1⁄2 inches, created around 1926.

**Creator:**
Harry Cimino produced this work, which is now housed in the Smithsonian American Art Museum's collection.

**Source Material & Literary Reference:**
The title references "Sutter's Gold," a literary work by Cendrars. The artwork depicts content related to the United States gold rush era, incorporating imagery of figures and a horse, suggesting themes of frontier adventure and historical exploration connected to this significant period in American history.

**Current Status:**
The piece is "Not on view" at the museum and was acquired as a "Gift of Charlotte Manzari" in 1969.

Based on the web search results, I found comprehensive information about Taryn Simon's work in the Smithsonian American Art Museum collection:

In Chapter X from "A Living Man Declared Dead and Other Chapters I-XVIII," Taryn Simon traced the bloodline of Cabrera Antero, one of the members of the Igorot community from the Philippines who were put on display at the Louisiana Purchase Exposition, which was a World's Fair held in St. Louis in 1904.

Simon located and photographed a majority of Antero's 158 descendants and relatives, whose diaspora spans the Philippines, the United States, Guam, Canada, New South Wales, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Vietnam and Japan.

The work is part of the Smithsonian American Art Museum collection (accession number 2014.26.1A-F), with the piece comprising six components of archival inkjet prints with overall dimensions of 84 x 304 1⁄4 inches (213.4 x 772.8 cm).

Chapter X, the multi-panel collage of Antero's lineage, is part of Simon's larger piece, A Living Man Declared Dead and Other Chapters: I-XVIII, which similarly archives the tales of seventeen other bloodlines from various origins and historically distinct circumstances. The work was produced over a four-year period (2008–11), during which the artist travelled around the world researching and documenting bloodlines and their related stories.

## Dissertation Structure

The dissertation is structured in three parts.

## Chapter Organization and Topics

In the introduction, three main desiderata for a theory of desire are formulated: the direction of fit (the intuition that the world should conform to our desires), the death of desire principle (the intuition that one cannot desire what one represents as actual), and desire's role in psychological explanations.

The first part examines the main conceptions of desire, with the first chapter devoted to the evaluative conception and the second examining the motivational approach.

A later chapter presents a typology of desires inspired by the deontic view and the types of norms there are, and the final chapter discusses the main objections to the deontic approach.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about the phrase "Logic of the Liver":

The phrase "Logic of the Liver" is a philosophical metaphor echoing Blaise Pascal's famous "Logic of the Heart," used to describe an inquiry into the nature of desire. The metaphor references the ancient tradition that the liver was thought to be the seat of desire, a tradition that started with Plato and remained influential in the Middle Ages.

The phrase was used in a 2014 PhD dissertation by Federico Lauria titled "The Logic of the Liver": A Deontic View of the Intentionality of Desire, which examines philosophical questions about how desires represent the world and their intentionality.

Lauria's dissertation proposes a deontic alternative to classical views of desire, arguing that desiring involves representing a state of affairs as what ought to be or should be, with desire involving a deontic manner of representing.

The phrase is a clever philosophical play on words that connects the classical understanding of the liver as the physical seat of desire (from ancient philosophy) with the logical/philosophical investigation of desire itself.

## Artist Biography

Harry Cimino was born in Marion, Indiana in 1898 and died in Sharon, Connecticut in 1969.

## "Sutter's Gold" Illustrations

The woodcut illustrations by Harry Cimino include chapter head and tail pieces, decorative chapter caps, and five color plates (counting the frontis.) More specifically, there are 5 full page "woodblocks in color"; 17 black-and-white woodcuts and 16 smaller woodcut designs at chapter ends.

## Publication Details

This is a reprint of the 1926 Harper & Row edition of Cendrars' novel. The book is a fictionalized account of the aftermath of the discovery of gold on Sutter's property in the Sierra Nevada foothills in 1848, which lead to the California Gold Rush of 1849.

The Smithsonian American Art Museum holds examples of Cimino's chapter heading woodcuts from this book in their collection, such as "Heading--Chapter XVII 'Sutter's Gold'" from ca. 1926, a woodcut measuring 2 1⁄8 x 3 1⁄2 in.

import math
def h(lat1,lon1,lat2,lon2):
    R=6371
    dl=math.radians(lat2-lat1)

    a=math.sin(dl/2)**2+math.cos(math.radians(lat1))*math.cos(math.radians(lat2))*math.sin(dL/2)**2
